abstract.para: Once &kdump; has captured a vmcore, use the crash utility to inspect it and find out what the kernel was doing at the moment it panicked.

step.para: Enable the product's Debug repository. It is disabled by default. List your repositories to find its exact alias, then enable it:
step.screen: &prompt.sudo; zypper lr | grep -i debug &prompt.sudo; zypper modifyrepo --enable DEBUG_REPO_ALIAS

step.para: Install crash and the debuginfo package matching your running kernel exactly:

note.title: The debuginfo package version must match the running kernel exactly
note.para: If kernel-default-debuginfo installs a version newer than the kernel you crashed (for example, because an update arrived after the crash but before you reboot), crash refuses to load it with a version mismatch error. Reboot onto the newest installed kernel first, and confirm uname -r matches the Kernel version line in the crash directory's README.txt before proceeding.

step.para: The debuginfo package alone is not enough: on &productnameshort;, its vmlinux.debug file contains only debug symbols, not the actual kernel code and data crash needs alongside them. Decompress the real kernel image from the matching kernel package and place it next to vmlinux.debug:

section.title: Opening the vmcore in crash
section.para: Start crash, giving it the kernel image you just placed and the captured vmcore:
Sample output, from a crash deliberately triggered as described in :
section.screen:
KERNEL: /usr/lib/debug/usr/lib/modules/6.12.0-160000.37-default/vmlinux DEBUGINFO: /usr/lib/debug/usr/lib/modules/6.12.0-160000.37-default/vmlinux.debug DUMPFILE: /var/crash/2026-09-10-11-33/vmcore [PARTIAL DUMP] CPUS: 2 DATE: Thu Sep 10 11:33:30 CEST 2026 UPTIME: 00:00:57 LOAD AVERAGE: 0.25, 0.08, 0.03 TASKS: 173 NODENAME: sles16 RELEASE: 6.12.0-160000.37-default VERSION: #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Aug 6 15:43:26 UTC 2026 (cf8ec7a) MACHINE: x86_64 (2304 Mhz) MEMORY: 4 GB PANIC: "Kernel panic - not syncing: sysrq triggered crash" PID: 4400 COMMAND: "tee" TASK: ffff8e020581c080 [THREAD_INFO: ffff8e020581c080] CPU: 0 STATE: TASK_RUNNING (PANIC)
crash> bt PID: 4400 TASK: ffff8e020581c080 CPU: 0 COMMAND: "tee" #0 [ffffd3de00e17928] machine_kexec at ffffffff94a95552 #1 [ffffd3de00e17988] __crash_kexec at ffffffff94bd61eb #2 [ffffd3de00e17a48] panic at ffffffff9572c8fd #3 [ffffd3de00e17ac8] sysrq_handle_crash at ffffffff9529e89a #4 [ffffd3de00e17ad0] __handle_sysrq.cold at ffffffff9576a328 #5 [ffffd3de00e17b00] write_sysrq_trigger at ffffffff9529f439 #6 [ffffd3de00e17b28] proc_reg_write at ffffffff94f0db9a #7 [ffffd3de00e17b40] vfs_write at ffffffff94e5c99b #8 [ffffd3de00e17bd8] ksys_write at ffffffff94e5d017 #9 [ffffd3de00e17c10] do_syscall_64 at ffffffff9578a94d #10 [ffffd3de00e17f40] entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe at ffffffff9580012f crash> quit

callout.para: The process that happened to be running when the crash was triggered, not necessarily a sign of a problem with that process. Here it is tee, because the crash in this example was deliberately triggered with echo c | sudo tee /proc/sysrq-trigger. On a real, unplanned crash this would show whatever command was running at the time.

section.para: The banner identifies the panic reason, the process that was running, and basic system information. bt without arguments shows the call stack of the process active at the moment of the crash, here showing the path from the sysrq-trigger write down to machine_kexec, which is &kexec; handing control to the capture kernel.

section.title: Useful follow-up commands

listitem.para: Lists the processes that were running at the moment of the crash.
Resolves a kernel symbol to its address, or an address back to a symbol.
Lists the open file descriptors of the current process.

section.para: crash has extensive built-in help: run help COMMAND inside a session for details on any of these.
